doc.title: David Murray interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 18, 2003

title: The string ballad concert and strings
summary: The Public Theater strings concert and the compliment from a couple whose child was conceived after it.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Yeah. Can’t get it out. I think that’s great. And you know emotion is something too, speaking about compliments, the biggest compliment that I ever had was a did a string concert one time at the Public Theater in New York. And I took the opportunity to — I did all ballads. It was me with strings, but it was all ballads. So like a couple of years after that I’m walking down St. Mark’s Place, a couple comes up to me and they say, “You see this kid? This kid was conceived after that concert.” And that was like the © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
highest — I was exalted. That was it. They knighted me right there. I’m still going from that.

So you know, if that human being came out of my string ballad concert — I mean there were actually people weeping in the concert. There’s something about strings that can make you go into it. But the whole thing is to do it without being maudlin. It can be contrived. You know strings, you can be cornball city with strings too, especially if you approach it from the ballad thing. Anyway, and that’s the whole thing about melody and song form, there’s a battle in the society right now because everybody’s more conditioned to hear beats. And the song form is getting a licking right now. When a guy like Stevie Wonder can’t come up with a hit, you know he’s a real songwriter. I mean I’m speaking in the black community particularly right now. When the community is like hoodwinked into thinking that this is only music. These beats, and this rap. This is what we call music now and this other stuff is maudlin and contrived because it is a melody. It sounds like, to them, somebody’s in a theater and then all of a sudden they break into song. And it’s corny. No it’s not corny. It’s a song. Songs will always be back. But it’s not here right now. And I think, I’m waiting for the time when the songwriter in the community will raise his head again.
